## **2. Required Kubernetes Files**

### **File 1: RayService Manifest** (Only Required File!)

**Create: `k8s/rayservice-local.yaml`**

```yaml
apiVersion: ray.io/v1
kind: RayService
metadata:
  name: embedding-service
  namespace: default
spec:
  serviceUnhealthySecondThreshold: 300
  deploymentUnhealthySecondThreshold: 300
  
  # Serve configuration
  serveConfigV2: |
    applications:
      - name: embedding-service
        import_path: src.service.ray_deployment:app
        route_prefix: /
  
  # Ray cluster configuration
  rayClusterConfig:
    rayVersion: '2.39.0'
    enableInTreeAutoscaling: true
    
    # Head node (no GPU)
    headGroupSpec:
      serviceType: ClusterIP
      rayStartParams:
        dashboard-host: '0.0.0.0'
        num-cpus: '0'
      template:
        spec:
          containers:
          - name: ray-head
            image: embedding-service:ray-latest  # Local image
            imagePullPolicy: Never  # ← CRITICAL: Don't try to pull from registry
            ports:
            - containerPort: 6379
              name: gcs
            - containerPort: 8265
              name: dashboard
            - containerPort: 10001
              name: client
            - containerPort: 8000
              name: serve
            resources:
              limits:
                cpu: "4"
                memory: "8Gi"
              requests:
                cpu: "2"
                memory: "4Gi"
            volumeMounts:
            - name: model-cache
              mountPath: /root/.cache/huggingface
          volumes:
          - name: model-cache
            persistentVolumeClaim:
              claimName: ray-storage-pvc
    
    # Worker nodes (GPU-enabled)
    workerGroupSpecs:
    - groupName: embedding-workers
      replicas: 2
      minReplicas: 2
      maxReplicas: 4
      rayStartParams:
        num-cpus: '0'
        num-gpus: '1'
      template:
        spec:
          containers:
          - name: ray-worker
            image: embedding-service:ray-latest  # Local image
            imagePullPolicy: Never  # ← CRITICAL: Don't try to pull
            lifecycle:
              preStop:
                exec:
                  command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "ray stop"]
            resources:
              limits:
                cpu: "8"
                memory: "16Gi"
                nvidia.com/gpu: "1"
              requests:
                cpu: "4"
                memory: "12Gi"
                nvidia.com/gpu: "1"
            volumeMounts:
            - name: model-cache
              mountPath: /root/.cache/huggingface
            env:
            - name: CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES
              value: "0"
          volumes:
          - name: model-cache
            persistentVolumeClaim:
              claimName: ray-storage-pvc
```

**Key differences for local deployment**:
- `imagePullPolicy: Never` - Critical! Tells K8s to use local image
- `image: embedding-service:ray-latest` - No registry prefix
- No `imagePullSecrets` needed

## **Simplified Kubernetes Work - Local Development**

### **What You DON'T Need** ❌
- ❌ Container registry (ECR, Docker Hub, etc.)
- ❌ Ingress controller
- ❌ DNS configuration
- ❌ TLS/SSL certificates
- ❌ ImagePullSecrets

### **What You DO Need** ✅

---

## **1. Load Docker Image into K8s Cluster**

Since your image is local, you need to make it available to your Kubernetes cluster:

### **Option A: If using Minikube**
```bash
# Use Minikube's Docker daemon
eval $(minikube docker-env)

# Build image (will be available in Minikube)
docker build -f Dockerfile.ray -t embedding-service:ray-latest .

# Verify
minikube ssh "docker images | grep embedding"
```

### **Option B: If using kind (Kubernetes in Docker)**
```bash
# Build image
docker build -f Dockerfile.ray -t embedding-service:ray-latest .

# Load into kind cluster
kind load docker-image embedding-service:ray-latest --name your-cluster-name

# Verify
docker exec -it your-cluster-name-control-plane crictl images | grep embedding
```

### **Option C: If using k3s/bare metal cluster**
```bash
# Build image on each node OR use local registry
docker build -f Dockerfile.ray -t embedding-service:ray-latest .

# Save and load on each node
docker save embedding-service:ray-latest | gzip > embedding-service.tar.gz
# Copy to each node and:
docker load < embedding-service.tar.gz
```

### **Option D: If using managed K8s (GKE, EKS, AKS) but testing locally**
```bash
# Set up local registry (runs in Docker)
docker run -d -p 5000:5000 --name registry registry:2

# Tag and push to local registry
docker tag embedding-service:ray-latest localhost:5000/embedding-service:ray-latest
docker push localhost:5000/embedding-service:ray-latest

# Use in K8s YAML: localhost:5000/embedding-service:ray-latest
```

---

## **2. Required Kubernetes Files**

### **File 1: RayService Manifest** (Only Required File!)

**Create: `k8s/rayservice-local.yaml`**

```yaml
apiVersion: ray.io/v1
kind: RayService
metadata:
  name: embedding-service
  namespace: default
spec:
  serviceUnhealthySecondThreshold: 300
  deploymentUnhealthySecondThreshold: 300
  
  # Serve configuration
  serveConfigV2: |
    applications:
      - name: embedding-service
        import_path: src.service.ray_deployment:app
        route_prefix: /
  
  # Ray cluster configuration
  rayClusterConfig:
    rayVersion: '2.39.0'
    enableInTreeAutoscaling: true
    
    # Head node (no GPU)
    headGroupSpec:
      serviceType: ClusterIP
      rayStartParams:
        dashboard-host: '0.0.0.0'
        num-cpus: '0'
      template:
        spec:
          containers:
          - name: ray-head
            image: embedding-service:ray-latest  # Local image
            imagePullPolicy: Never  # ← CRITICAL: Don't try to pull from registry
            ports:
            - containerPort: 6379
              name: gcs
            - containerPort: 8265
              name: dashboard
            - containerPort: 10001
              name: client
            - containerPort: 8000
              name: serve
            resources:
              limits:
                cpu: "4"
                memory: "8Gi"
              requests:
                cpu: "2"
                memory: "4Gi"
            volumeMounts:
            - name: model-cache
              mountPath: /root/.cache/huggingface
          volumes:
          - name: model-cache
            persistentVolumeClaim:
              claimName: ray-storage-pvc
    
    # Worker nodes (GPU-enabled)
    workerGroupSpecs:
    - groupName: embedding-workers
      replicas: 2
      minReplicas: 2
      maxReplicas: 4
      rayStartParams:
        num-cpus: '0'
        num-gpus: '1'
      template:
        spec:
          containers:
          - name: ray-worker
            image: embedding-service:ray-latest  # Local image
            imagePullPolicy: Never  # ← CRITICAL: Don't try to pull
            lifecycle:
              preStop:
                exec:
                  command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "ray stop"]
            resources:
              limits:
                cpu: "8"
                memory: "16Gi"
                nvidia.com/gpu: "1"
              requests:
                cpu: "4"
                memory: "12Gi"
                nvidia.com/gpu: "1"
            volumeMounts:
            - name: model-cache
              mountPath: /root/.cache/huggingface
            env:
            - name: CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES
              value: "0"
          volumes:
          - name: model-cache
            persistentVolumeClaim:
              claimName: ray-storage-pvc
```

**Key differences for local deployment**:
- `imagePullPolicy: Never` - Critical! Tells K8s to use local image
- `image: embedding-service:ray-latest` - No registry prefix
- No `imagePullSecrets` needed

  - Create new file src/service/ray_deployment.py that wraps the existing FastAPI app with @serve.deployment and @serve.ingress decorators. This is ~25 lines and requires zero changes to existing code. The wrapper enables Ray Serve to load balance across replicas while preserving all routes, middleware, and business logic.
- [ ] Create Dockerfile.ray for Ray-enabled image
  - Create Dockerfile.ray that extends rayproject/ray:2.39.0-py311-gpu base image. Copy application code into /app, install dependencies, and set WORKDIR. No CMD needed as KubeRay will run 'ray start' automatically. Image will be built locally (no registry push needed for development).
- [ ] Create k8s/rayservice-local.yaml manifest
  - Create RayService Kubernetes manifest with: serveConfigV2 pointing to src.service.ray_deployment:app, headGroupSpec (4 CPU, 8GB RAM, no GPU), workerGroupSpecs (2-4 replicas, 1 GPU each), imagePullPolicy: Never for local images, volumeMounts for ray-storage-pvc at /root/.cache/huggingface. Includes autoscaling config (min: 2, max: 16 replicas) and Ray actor options (num_gpus: 0.5, num_cpus: 2).
- [ ] Create k8s/ directory if not exists
  - Create the k8s/ directory in the project root to hold Kubernetes manifests (rayservice-local.yaml and any future configs).
- [ ] Build Docker image locally
  - Run: docker build -f Dockerfile.ray -t embedding-service:ray-latest . Verify image exists with: docker images | grep embedding-service. Image will be ~8GB (includes Ray, PyTorch, Transformers, and application code).
- [ ] Load image into Kubernetes cluster
  - Make local Docker image available to K8s cluster. For kind: 'kind load docker-image embedding-service:ray-latest'. For Minikube: build using 'eval $(minikube docker-env)' first. For other setups: may need local registry or build on each node. Verify with appropriate cluster image list command.
- [ ] Verify Kubernetes prerequisites
  - Check: 1) KubeRay operator running (kubectl get pods -n kuberay-system), 2) PVC ray-storage-pvc exists and is Bound (kubectl get pvc), 3) GPU nodes available (kubectl get nodes with nvidia.com/gpu capacity). All should already be configured based on existing ray-cluster-dual-workers.yaml.
- [ ] Deploy RayService to Kubernetes
  - Run: kubectl apply -f k8s/rayservice-local.yaml. This creates the Ray cluster (head + 2 workers), deploys Serve application, and creates services. Monitor with: kubectl get rayservices -w until STATUS shows 'Running'.
- [ ] Verify pods are created and running
  - Check pods with: kubectl get pods -l ray.io/cluster=embedding-service. Should see: 1 head pod, 2 worker pods (initial replicas), all in Running state. Check logs: kubectl logs embedding-service-raycluster-*-head-* for Serve deployment status.

  - Run: kubectl port-forward svc/embedding-service-serve-svc 8000:8000. Test endpoints: curl http://localhost:8000/health/ready, curl -X POST http://localhost:8000/embeddings with test data. Verify all existing endpoints work (embeddings, similarity, health, models).

  - Generate load (multiple concurrent requests) and watch: kubectl get pods -l ray.io/cluster=embedding-service -w. Verify Ray Serve scales replicas up (toward max 16) under load and down (toward min 2) when idle. Check replica count in Ray Dashboard Serve tab.
- [ ] Document deployment workflow
  - Update README.md or create DEPLOYMENT.md with: local development setup, Docker image build process, K8s deployment steps, testing procedures, troubleshooting tips. Include commands for rebuilding/redeploying after code changes.
- [ ] Optional: Create ConfigMap for configuration

**Base**: `debian:bookworm-slim`

Install only:

- pip
- ray[serve]

**Advantage**: Maximum control, smallest possible size
**Disadvantage**: More manual Python setup

### **Option 3: Multi-stage Build** (~3.5GB final)

Build dependencies in one stage, copy only runtime to final stage:

```dockerfile
# Stage 1: Builder (discarded)
FROM python:3.12 as builder
# Install build tools, compile wheels
# Create virtual environment

# Stage 2: Runtime (kept)
FROM python:3.12-slim
# Copy only the virtual environment
# No build tools, no compilers
```

**Advantage**: Clean separation, no build artifacts
**Disadvantage**: Slightly more complex

---

## **Recommended Approach: Option 1 (Python Slim + Ray)**

### **Architecture**:

```dockerfile
FROM python:3.12-slim

# Install system dependencies (minimal)
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y \
    git \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

WORKDIR /app

# Copy and install Python dependencies
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

# Install Ray Serve (separate for clarity)
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir "ray[serve]==2.39.0"

# Copy application code
COPY src/ /app/src/
COPY setup.py pyproject.toml /app/
RUN pip install -e .

# KubeRay will run: ray start --head --port=6379 --dashboard-host=0.0.0.0
```

### **Why This Works**:

1. **CUDA from host**: K8s passes GPU via `--gpus` flag → NVIDIA container toolkit mounts host CUDA libraries
2. **PyTorch uses host CUDA**: Your existing
in

will use host CUDA runtime
3. **Ray doesn't need CUDA directly**: Ray just coordinates workers, doesn't do GPU ops itself
4. **Proven pattern**: Your current

(for non-Ray version) already does this successfully

|----------|------|-----|---------|--------------|-----|-----------|
| **Official Ray GPU** | 11GB | included | included | ❌ | +0.1GB | **~11GB** |
| **Python Slim (Rec.)** | 0.15GB | 0.5GB | 0.9GB | 0.1GB | 0.1GB | **~3.5GB** |
| **Debian Slim** | 0.08GB | 0.5GB | 0.9GB | 0.1GB | 0.1GB | **~3.2GB** |
| **Multi-stage** | 0.15GB | 0.5GB | 0.9GB | 0.1GB | 0.1GB | **~3.5GB** |

**Space savings: ~7.5GB (68% reduction)**

### **1. Ray Version Compatibility**
- Your KubeRay operator version must match Ray runtime version
- Check: `kubectl get crd rayclusters.ray.io -o yaml | grep version`
- If operator is 2.39.0, Ray 2.39.0 works ✅

### **2. CUDA Runtime Requirements**

Ray Serve itself **doesn't need CUDA**, but your PyTorch operations do:

**What gets mounted from host** (via `--gpus`):
- NVIDIA driver
- CUDA runtime libraries (`libcuda.so`, `libnvidia-ml.so`)
- cuDNN libraries

**What PyTorch needs in container**:
- Python bindings to CUDA (part of PyTorch wheel)
- C++ CUDA libraries ← **mounted from host**

```bash
# Check if your requirements.txt has GPU-enabled PyTorch

```

- `ray-core` (scheduler, actor system)

Excellent point! You're absolutely right - the official Ray GPU images are bloated with Anaconda, TensorFlow, and tons of ML frameworks you don't need. Let's design a **slim custom base image strategy**.

---

## **Image Bloat Analysis**

### **Official `rayproject/ray:2.39.0-py311-gpu`** (~11GB):
- ❌ Anaconda/Conda (~2-3GB)
- ❌ TensorFlow (~2GB)
- ❌ Multiple CUDA toolkits
- ❌ Jupyter, notebooks, examples
- ❌ Pre-installed ML frameworks you don't use
- ✅ Ray runtime (~500MB)
- ✅ Python 3.11

### **What You Actually Need**:
- ✅ Python 3.12 (matching your local dev)
- ✅ `ray[serve]==2.39.0` (~500MB installed)
- ✅ Your existing dependencies (PyTorch, Transformers, FastAPI - **already in your requirements.txt**)
- ✅ CUDA runtime libraries (can use host's NVIDIA toolkit via `--gpus` flag)

---

## **Slim Image Strategy Options**

### **Option 1: Pure Python Slim Base** (Recommended - ~3-4GB final)

**Base**: `python:3.12-slim` (same as your current Dockerfile)

**Why this works**:
```
python:3.12-slim (150MB)
  ↓
+ ray[serve]==2.39.0 (~500MB with dependencies)
  ↓
+ Your requirements.txt:
  - torch (~900MB - you already have this)
  - transformers (~100MB - you already have this)
  - fastapi, uvicorn, etc. (~50MB - you already have this)
  ↓
+ Your application code (~10MB)
  ↓
= ~3.5GB total (vs 11GB Ray official image)
```

**Key insight**: 
- You **don't need CUDA in the container** - host NVIDIA toolkit provides it via `--gpus` flag
- Ray just needs to run, it doesn't need all the ML frameworks
- Your app dependencies (PyTorch) already handle GPU operations

### **Option 2: Debian Slim Base** (~3GB final)

**Base**: `debian:bookworm-slim`

Install only:
- Python 3.12 (from apt)
- pip
- ray[serve]
- Your dependencies

**Advantage**: Maximum control, smallest possible size
**Disadvantage**: More manual Python setup

### **Option 3: Multi-stage Build** (~3.5GB final)

Build dependencies in one stage, copy only runtime to final stage:

```dockerfile
# Stage 1: Builder (discarded)
FROM python:3.12 as builder
# Install build tools, compile wheels
# Create virtual environment

# Stage 2: Runtime (kept)
FROM python:3.12-slim
# Copy only the virtual environment
# No build tools, no compilers
```

**Advantage**: Clean separation, no build artifacts
**Disadvantage**: Slightly more complex

---

## **Recommended Approach: Option 1 (Python Slim + Ray)**

### **Architecture**:

```dockerfile
FROM python:3.12-slim

# Install system dependencies (minimal)
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y \
    git \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

WORKDIR /app

# Copy and install Python dependencies
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

# Install Ray Serve (separate for clarity)
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir "ray[serve]==2.39.0"

# Copy application code
COPY src/ /app/src/
COPY setup.py pyproject.toml /app/
RUN pip install -e .

# KubeRay will run: ray start --head --port=6379 --dashboard-host=0.0.0.0
```

### **Why This Works**:

1. **CUDA from host**: K8s passes GPU via `--gpus` flag → NVIDIA container toolkit mounts host CUDA libraries
2. **PyTorch uses host CUDA**: Your existing `torch` in requirements.txt will use host CUDA runtime
3. **Ray doesn't need CUDA directly**: Ray just coordinates workers, doesn't do GPU ops itself
4. **Proven pattern**: Your current `Dockerfile` (for non-Ray version) already does this successfully

---

## **Size Comparison**

| Approach | Base | Ray | PyTorch | Transformers | App | **Total** |
|----------|------|-----|---------|--------------|-----|-----------|
| **Official Ray GPU** | 11GB | included | included | ❌ | +0.1GB | **~11GB** |
| **Python Slim (Rec.)** | 0.15GB | 0.5GB | 0.9GB | 0.1GB | 0.1GB | **~3.5GB** |
| **Debian Slim** | 0.08GB | 0.5GB | 0.9GB | 0.1GB | 0.1GB | **~3.2GB** |
| **Multi-stage** | 0.15GB | 0.5GB | 0.9GB | 0.1GB | 0.1GB | **~3.5GB** |

**Space savings: ~7.5GB (68% reduction)**

---

## **Critical Considerations**

### **1. Ray Version Compatibility**
- Your KubeRay operator version must match Ray runtime version
- Check: `kubectl get crd rayclusters.ray.io -o yaml | grep version`
- If operator is 2.39.0, Ray 2.39.0 works ✅

### **2. CUDA Runtime Requirements**

Ray Serve itself **doesn't need CUDA**, but your PyTorch operations do:

**What gets mounted from host** (via `--gpus`):
- NVIDIA driver
- CUDA runtime libraries (`libcuda.so`, `libnvidia-ml.so`)
- cuDNN libraries

**What PyTorch needs in container**:
- Python bindings to CUDA (part of PyTorch wheel)
- C++ CUDA libraries ← **mounted from host**

**Verify your PyTorch wheel**:
```bash
# Check if your requirements.txt has GPU-enabled PyTorch
cat requirements.txt | grep torch

# Should be something like:
# torch==2.x.x+cu121  (CUDA 12.1)
# OR
# torch==2.x.x  (will auto-detect CUDA from host)
```

### **3. Ray Serve Dependencies**

`ray[serve]` includes:
- `ray-core` (scheduler, actor system)
- `aiohttp`, `aiosignal` (async HTTP)
- `fastapi` (might duplicate your existing one - OK)
- `uvicorn` (server)
- `pydantic` (already in your deps)

**Potential conflicts**: None expected, Ray uses compatible versions

---

## **Testing Strategy**

### **Phase 1: Test Slim Image Locally**

```bash
# Build slim image
docker build -f Dockerfile.ray-slim -t embedding-service:ray-slim .

# Test Ray starts
docker run --rm embedding-service:ray-slim ray start --head --block

# Test with GPU
docker run --rm --gpus all embedding-service:ray-slim python -c "import torch; print(torch.cuda.is_available())"
```

### **Phase 2: Test Ray Serve Locally**

```bash
# Run Ray Serve
docker run --rm --gpus all -p 8000:8000 embedding-service:ray-slim \
  serve run src.service.ray_deployment:app

# Test endpoints
curl http://localhost:8000/health/ready
```

### **Phase 3: Deploy to K8s**

If local tests pass, deploy to cluster.

---

## **Potential Issues & Mitigations**

### **Issue 1: Missing System Libraries**

**Symptom**: `ImportError: libcudart.so.12 not found`

**Solution**: Host NVIDIA toolkit should provide this, but if missing:
```dockerfile
# Add CUDA runtime (not full toolkit)
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y cuda-runtime-12-0
```

**Better solution**: Ensure K8s nodes have NVIDIA container toolkit installed

### **Issue 2: Ray Version Mismatch**

**Symptom**: `RayService` fails to deploy, operator logs show version incompatibility

**Solution**: Match Ray version exactly:
```bash
# Check operator version
kubectl get deployment kuberay-operator -n kuberay-system -o yaml | grep image:

# Install matching Ray version
pip install ray[serve]==<exact-version>
```

### **Issue 3: Python Version Mismatch**

**Symptom**: Import errors, incompatible bytecode

**Solution**: Your local dev is Python 3.12.1, use same in container (already planned)

---

## **Updated Plan**

### **Build Strategy**:

1. **Base**: `python:3.12-slim` (150MB)
2. **Add**: System deps (`git` only, ~50MB)
3. **Add**: Your existing `requirements.txt` (PyTorch, Transformers, FastAPI, ~1.5GB)
4. **Add**: `ray[serve]==2.39.0` (~500MB)
5. **Add**: Your application code (~10MB)
6. **Total**: ~3.5GB (vs 11GB official Ray image)

### **Space Math Updated**:

- Current available: 12GB on `/`
- Need to download: ~0.5GB (Ray wheels, since you have Python/PyTorch base layers)
- Build artifacts: ~1GB temporary
- Final image: ~3.5GB
- **Should fit comfortably** ✅

---

## **Dockerfile Structure (Conceptual)**

```dockerfile
# Slim base (reuses your existing image layers)
FROM python:3.12-slim

# Minimal system deps
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y git && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

WORKDIR /app

# Install your app dependencies first (leverage layer caching)
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

# Add Ray Serve (separate layer for easy updates)
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir "ray[serve]==2.39.0"

# Copy application code
COPY src/ /app/src/
COPY setup.py pyproject.toml /app/
RUN pip install -e .

# Ray start command handled by KubeRay
```

**Layer caching benefit**: If you rebuild after code changes, only the last layers rebuild (~10MB), not the 3GB of dependencies.

---

## **Recommendation**

**Go with Option 1 (Python Slim)** because:

1. ✅ **68% smaller** than official Ray image
2. ✅ **Fits in available space** (12GB - 3.5GB = 8.5GB headroom)
3. ✅ **Reuses existing Dockerfile pattern** (you already use `python:3.12-slim`)
4. ✅ **Host NVIDIA toolkit provides CUDA** (proven by your existing container)
5. ✅ **Layer caching** from your current `embedding-service:latest` image
6. ✅ **Simple to maintain** (just add Ray to existing build)

**This should build successfully with your current disk space.**

response.invocationMessage: Using "Manage and track todo items for task planning"

todoList.title: Add ray[serve]==2.39.0 to requirements.in
todoList.description: Add 'ray[serve]==2.39.0' as a dependency in requirements.in. This will include Ray core and serve components needed for deployment.

todoList.title: Compile requirements.txt from requirements.in
todoList.description: Run 'pip-compile requirements.in' to generate requirements.txt with all Ray dependencies resolved. This ensures pinned versions for reproducible builds.

todoList.title: Create Ray Serve deployment wrapper
todoList.description: Create src/service/ray_deployment.py (~25 lines) that wraps existing FastAPI app with @serve.deployment and @serve.ingress decorators. Zero changes to existing code needed. Format: import app from main, wrap with decorators, expose for Ray Serve.

todoList.title: Build Docker image with existing Dockerfile
todoList.description: Run 'docker build -t embedding-service:ray-latest .' using the existing Dockerfile. Since Ray is now in requirements.txt, the current CUDA-based Dockerfile will build an image with all dependencies including Ray Serve. No Dockerfile changes needed.

todoList.title: Create k8s/ directory
todoList.description: Create k8s/ directory in project root to hold Kubernetes manifests.

todoList.title: Create k8s/rayservice-local.yaml manifest
todoList.description: Create RayService manifest with: serveConfigV2 pointing to src.service.ray_deployment:app, headGroupSpec (4 CPU, 8GB RAM, no GPU), workerGroupSpecs (2-4 replicas, 1 GPU each, 0.5 GPU per replica), imagePullPolicy: Never, volumeMounts for ray-storage-pvc at /root/.cache/huggingface, autoscaling (min: 2, max: 16).

todoList.title: Load image into Kubernetes cluster
todoList.description: Make local Docker image available to K8s. For kind: 'kind load docker-image embedding-service:ray-latest'. For minikube: use 'eval $(minikube docker-env)' then rebuild. Verify with cluster-specific image list command.

todoList.title: Verify Kubernetes prerequisites
todoList.description: Check: 1) KubeRay operator running (kubectl get pods -n kuberay-system), 2) PVC ray-storage-pvc exists and Bound (kubectl get pvc), 3) GPU nodes available (kubectl get nodes with nvidia.com/gpu). Should already be configured from existing ray-cluster-dual-workers.yaml.

todoList.title: Deploy RayService to Kubernetes
todoList.description: Run 'kubectl apply -f k8s/rayservice-local.yaml'. Monitor with 'kubectl get rayservices -w' until STATUS shows 'Running'. This creates Ray cluster (head + workers) and deploys Serve application.

todoList.title: Verify pods running
todoList.description: Check 'kubectl get pods -l ray.io/cluster=embedding-service'. Should see 1 head pod + 2 worker pods (initial replicas) all Running. Check logs: 'kubectl logs embedding-service-raycluster-*-head-*' for Serve deployment confirmation.

todoList.title: Test service via port-forward
todoList.description: Port-forward: 'kubectl port-forward svc/embedding-service-serve-svc 8000:8000'. Test: curl http://localhost:8000/health/ready, POST to /embeddings with sample data. Verify all existing endpoints work (embeddings, similarity, health, models).

todoList.title: Verify Ray Dashboard access
todoList.description: Port-forward Dashboard: 'kubectl port-forward svc/embedding-service-head-svc 8265:8265'. Open http://localhost:8265. Check Serve tab shows deployment with replicas healthy, verify GPU utilization and replica distribution across workers.

todoList.title: Test autoscaling behavior
todoList.description: Generate load (concurrent requests) and watch 'kubectl get pods -l ray.io/cluster=embedding-service -w'. Verify Ray Serve scales replicas up (toward max 16) under load and down (toward min 2) when idle. Monitor in Ray Dashboard Serve tab.

todoList.title: Document deployment workflow
todoList.description: Update README.md or create DEPLOYMENT.md with: requirements compilation, Docker build, K8s deployment, testing, troubleshooting. Include rebuild/redeploy workflow after code changes.

{"filePath": "/home/electric/workspace/EmbeddingService/src/service/ray_deployment.py", "content": """"
Ray Serve deployment wrapper for EmbeddingService.

This module wraps the existing FastAPI application with Ray Serve
decorators to enable distributed deployment with autoscaling and
load balancing. No changes to the existing application logic required.
"""

from ray import serve

# Import the existing FastAPI app
from src.service.main import app


@serve.deployment(
    name="embedding-service",
    num_replicas=2,  # Initial replicas (will be overridden by autoscaling config in K8s)
    ray_actor_options={
        "num_cpus": 2,
        "num_gpus": 0.5,  # Allow 2 replicas per GPU
    },
    autoscaling_config={
        "min_replicas": 2,
        "max_replicas": 16,
        "target_num_ongoing_requests_per_replica": 4,
    },
)
@serve.ingress(app)
class EmbeddingServiceDeployment:
    """
    Ray Serve deployment that wraps the FastAPI application.
    
    The @serve.ingress decorator makes all FastAPI routes available
    through Ray Serve, preserving all existing endpoints, middleware,
    and business logic without modification.
    """
    pass


# Deployment binding for Ray Serve
deployment = EmbeddingServiceDeployment.bind()
"}

toolCalls.arguments:
{"filePath": "/home/electric/workspace/EmbeddingService/k8s/rayservice-local.yaml", "content": "apiVersion: ray.io/v1
kind: RayService
metadata:
  name: embedding-service
  namespace: default
spec:
  serviceUnhealthySecondThreshold: 900
  deploymentUnhealthySecondThreshold: 300
  
  # Ray Serve application configuration
  serveConfigV2: |
    applications:
      - name: embedding-service
        import_path: src.service.ray_deployment:deployment
        runtime_env:
          working_dir: "."
          pip:
            - ray[serve]==2.39.0
        deployments:
          - name: embedding-service
            num_replicas: 2
            ray_actor_options:
              num_cpus: 2
              num_gpus: 0.5
            autoscaling_config:
              min_replicas: 2
              max_replicas: 16
              target_num_ongoing_requests_per_replica: 4
  
  # Ray Cluster configuration
  rayClusterConfig:
    rayVersion: '2.39.0'
    
    # Head node - no GPU, used for coordination
    headGroupSpec:
      serviceType: ClusterIP
      rayStartParams:
        dashboard-host: '0.0.0.0'
        num-cpus: '0'
      template:
        spec:
          containers:
          - name: ray-head
            image: embedding-service:ray-latest
            imagePullPolicy: Never  # Use local image
            ports:
            - containerPort: 6379
              name: gcs
            - containerPort: 8265
              name: dashboard
            - containerPort: 10001
              name: client
            - containerPort: 8000
              name: serve
            resources:
              limits:
                cpu: "4"
                memory: "8Gi"
              requests:
                cpu: "2"
                memory: "4Gi"
            volumeMounts:
            - name: huggingface-cache
              mountPath: /root/.cache/huggingface
            env:
            - name: RAY_STORAGE_PATH
              value: "/mnt/ray-storage"
            - name: TRANSFORMERS_CACHE
              value: "/root/.cache/huggingface"
          volumes:
          - name: huggingface-cache
            persistentVolumeClaim:
              claimName: ray-storage-pvc
    
    # Worker nodes - GPU enabled for embedding operations
    workerGroupSpecs:
    - groupName: gpu-workers
      replicas: 2
      minReplicas: 2
      maxReplicas: 4
      rayStartParams:
        num-gpus: '1'
      template:
        spec:
          containers:
          - name: ray-worker
            image: embedding-service:ray-latest
            imagePullPolicy: Never  # Use local image
            lifecycle:
              preStop:
                exec:
                  command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "ray stop"]
            resources:
              limits:
                cpu: "6"
                memory: "16Gi"
                nvidia.com/gpu: "1"
              requests:
                cpu: "3"
                memory: "8Gi"
                nvidia.com/gpu: "1"
            volumeMounts:
            - name: huggingface-cache
              mountPath: /root/.cache/huggingface
            env:
            - name: RAY_STORAGE_PATH
              value: "/mnt/ray-storage"
            - name: TRANSFORMERS_CACHE
              value: "/root/.cache/huggingface"
            - name: NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES
              value: "all"
            - name: CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES
              value: "0"
          volumes:
          - name: huggingface-cache
            persistentVolumeClaim:
              claimName: ray-storage-pvc
"}

toolCallRounds.response: Image is 7.96GB - fits well within available disk space! Now let's check which K8s cluster type we have (kind, minikube, or other) and load the image:

toolCalls.name: run_in_terminal
toolCalls.arguments: {"command": "kubectl config current-context", "explanation": "Checking which Kubernetes cluster is currently active", "isBackground": false}

toolCallRounds.response: This looks like a standard Kubernetes cluster (not kind or minikube). Let me check the node setup to understand how to make the local image available:

toolCalls.name: run_in_terminal
toolCalls.arguments: {"command": "kubectl get nodes -o wide", "explanation": "Checking cluster nodes to understand the setup", "isBackground": false}

toolCallRounds.response: Single-node cluster with containerd runtime. Since we're on a single node and the image is already in the local Docker daemon, we need to import it into containerd. Let me check if this is possible:

toolCalls.name: run_in_terminal
toolCalls.arguments: {"command": "which ctr && which crictl", "explanation": "Checking for containerd tools to import Docker image", "isBackground": false}

toolCallRounds.response: Perfect! We have `ctr` available. Let's export from Docker and import to containerd:

toolCalls.name: run_in_terminal
toolCalls.arguments: {"command": "docker save embedding-service:ray-latest | sudo ctr -n k8s.io images import -", "explanation": "Exporting Docker image and importing into containerd namespace for Kubernetes", "isBackground": false}

Ray Serve: Scalable and Programmable Serving
Production Guide
Deploy on Kubernetes
Deploy on Kubernetes
This section should help you:

understand how to install and use the KubeRay operator.
understand how to deploy a Ray Serve application using a RayService.
understand how to monitor and update your application.
Deploying Ray Serve on Kubernetes provides the scalable compute of Ray Serve and operational benefits of Kubernetes. This combination also allows you to integrate with existing applications that may be running on Kubernetes. When running on Kubernetes, use the RayService controller from KubeRay.

NOTE: Anyscale is a managed Ray solution that provides high-availability, high-performance autoscaling, multi-cloud clusters, spot instance support, and more out of the box.
A RayService CR encapsulates a multi-node Ray Cluster and a Serve application that runs on top of it into a single Kubernetes manifest. Deploying, upgrading, and getting the status of the application can be done using standard kubectl commands. This section walks through how to deploy, monitor, and upgrade the Text ML example on Kubernetes.

Installing the KubeRay operator

Follow the KubeRay quickstart guide to:

Install kubectl and Helm
Prepare a Kubernetes cluster
Deploy a KubeRay operator
Setting up a RayService custom resource (CR)

Once the KubeRay controller is running, manage your Ray Serve application by creating and updating a RayService CR (example).

Under the spec section in the RayService CR, set the following fields:

serveConfigV2: Represents the configuration that Ray Serve uses to deploy the application. Using serve build to print the Serve configuration and copy-paste it directly into your Kubernetes config and RayService CR.

rayClusterConfig: Populate this field with the contents of the spec field from the RayCluster CR YAML file. Refer to KubeRay configuration for more details.

Tip
To enhance the reliability of your application, particularly when dealing with large dependencies that may require a significant amount of time to download, consider including the dependencies in your image’s Dockerfile, so the dependencies are available as soon as the pods start.
Deploying a Serve application

When the RayService is created, the KubeRay controller first creates a Ray cluster using the provided configuration. Then, once the cluster is running, it deploys the Serve application to the cluster using the REST API. The controller also creates a Kubernetes Service that can be used to route traffic to the Serve application.

To see an example, deploy the Text ML example. The Serve config for the example is embedded into this sample RayService CR. Save this CR locally to a file named ray-service.text-ml.yaml:

Note
The example RayService uses very low numCpus values for demonstration purposes. In production, provide more resources to the Serve application. Learn more about how to configure KubeRay clusters here.
If you have dependencies that must be installed during deployment, you can add them to the runtime_env in the Deployment code. Learn more here
curl -o ray-service.text-ml.yaml https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ray-project/kuberay/2ba0dd7bea387ac9df3681666bab3d622e89846c/ray-operator/config/samples/ray-service.text-ml.yaml

To deploy the example, we simply kubectl apply the CR. This creates the underlying Ray cluster, consisting of a head and worker node pod (see Ray Clusters Key Concepts for more details on Ray clusters), as well as the service that can be used to query our application:

kubectl apply -f ray-service.text-ml.yaml

kubectl get rayservices
NAME                SERVICE STATUS   NUM SERVE ENDPOINTS
rayservice-sample   Running          1

kubectl get pods
NAME                                                          READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
rayservice-sample-raycluster-7wlx2-head-hr8mg                 1/1     Running   0          XXs
rayservice-sample-raycluster-7wlx2-small-group-worker-tb8nn   1/1     Running   0          XXs

kubectl get services
NAME                                          TYPE        CLUSTER-IP        EXTERNAL-IP   PORT(S)                                         AGE
rayservice-sample-head-svc                    ClusterIP   None              <none>        10001/TCP,8265/TCP,6379/TCP,8080/TCP,8000/TCP   XXs
rayservice-sample-raycluster-7wlx2-head-svc   ClusterIP   None              <none>        10001/TCP,8265/TCP,6379/TCP,8080/TCP,8000/TCP   XXs
rayservice-sample-serve-svc                   ClusterIP   192.168.145.219   <none>        8000/TCP                                        XXs

Note that the rayservice-sample-serve-svc above is the one that can be used to send queries to the Serve application – this will be used in the next section.

Querying the application

Once the RayService is running, we can query it over HTTP using the service created by the KubeRay controller. This service can be queried directly from inside the cluster, but to access it from your laptop you’ll need to configure a Kubernetes ingress or use port forwarding as below:

kubectl port-forward service/rayservice-sample-serve-svc 8000
curl -X POST -H "Content-Type: application/json" localhost:8000/summarize_translate -d '"It was the best of times, it was the worst of times, it was the age of wisdom, it was the age of foolishness, it was the epoch of belief"'
c'était le meilleur des temps, c'était le pire des temps .

Getting the status of the application

As the RayService is running, the KubeRay controller continually monitors it and writes relevant status updates to the CR. You can view the status of the application using kubectl describe. This includes the status of the cluster, events such as health check failures or restarts, and the application-level statuses reported by serve status.

kubectl get rayservices
NAME                AGE
rayservice-sample   7s

kubectl describe rayservice rayservice-sample
...
Status:
  Active Service Status:
    Ray Cluster Status:
      Available Worker Replicas:  1
      Desired CPU:                2500m
      Desired GPU:                0
      Desired Memory:             4Gi
      Desired TPU:                0
      Desired Worker Replicas:    1
      Endpoints:
        Client:     10001
        Dashboard:  8265

        Redis:      6379

        Pod IP:             10.48.99.153

        Service IP:         10.48.99.153

Events:

  ----    ------   ----                     ----                   -------
  Normal  Running  2m15s (x29791 over 16h)  rayservice-controller  The Serve applicaton is now running and healthy.

Updating the application

To update the RayService, modify the manifest and apply it use kubectl apply. There are two types of updates that can occur:

Application-level updates: when only the Serve config options are changed, the update is applied in-place on the same Ray cluster. This enables lightweight updates such as scaling a deployment up or down or modifying autoscaling parameters.
Cluster-level updates: when the RayCluster config options are changed, such as updating the container image for the cluster, it may result in a cluster-level update. In this case, a new cluster is started, and the application is deployed to it. Once the new cluster is ready, the Kubernetes service is updated to point to the new cluster and the previous cluster is terminated. There should not be any downtime for the application, but note that this requires the Kubernetes cluster to be large enough to schedule both Ray clusters.
Example: Serve config update

In the Text ML example above, change the language of the Translator in the Serve config to German:

  - name: Translator
    num_replicas: 1
    user_config:
      language: german

Now to update the application we apply the modified manifest:

kubectl apply -f ray-service.text-ml.yaml

kubectl describe rayservice rayservice-sample
...
  Serve Deployment Statuses:
    text_ml_app_Translator:
      Health Last Update Time:  2023-09-07T18:21:36Z
      Last Update Time:         2023-09-07T18:21:36Z
      Status:                   UPDATING
...

Query the application to see a different translation in German:

curl -X POST -H "Content-Type: application/json" localhost:8000/summarize_translate -d '"It was the best of times, it was the worst of times, it was the age of wisdom, it was the age of foolishness, it was the epoch of belief"'
Es war die beste Zeit, es war die schlimmste Zeit .

Updating the RayCluster config

The process of updating the RayCluster config is the same as updating the Serve config. For example, we can update the number of worker nodes to 2 in the manifest:

workerGroupSpecs:
the number of pods in the worker group.
  - replicas: 2

kubectl apply -f ray-service.text-ml.yaml

kubectl describe rayservice rayservice-sample
...
  pendingServiceStatus:
    appStatus: {}
    dashboardStatus:
      healthLastUpdateTime: "2022-07-18T21:54:53Z"
      lastUpdateTime: "2022-07-18T21:54:54Z"
    rayClusterName: rayservice-sample-raycluster-bshfr
    rayClusterStatus: {}
...

In the status, you can see that the RayService is preparing a pending cluster. After the pending cluster is healthy, it becomes the active cluster and the previous cluster is terminated.

Autoscaling

You can configure autoscaling for your Serve application by setting the autoscaling field in the Serve config. Learn more about the configuration options in the Serve Autoscaling Guide.

To enable autoscaling in a KubeRay Cluster, you need to set enableInTreeAutoscaling to True. Additionally, there are other options available to configure the autoscaling behavior. For further details, please refer to the documentation here.

Note
In most use cases, it is recommended to enable Kubernetes autoscaling to fully utilize the resources in your cluster. If you are using GKE, you can utilize the AutoPilot Kubernetes cluster. For instructions, see Create an Autopilot Cluster. For EKS, you can enable Kubernetes cluster autoscaling by utilizing the Cluster Autoscaler. For detailed information, see Cluster Autoscaler on AWS. To understand the relationship between Kubernetes autoscaling and Ray autoscaling, see Ray Autoscaler with Kubernetes Cluster Autoscaler.
Load balancer

Set up ingress to expose your Serve application with a load balancer. See this configuration

Note
Ray Serve runs HTTP proxy on every node, allowing you to use /-/routes as the endpoint for node health checks.
Ray Serve uses port 8000 as the default HTTP proxy traffic port. You can change the port by setting http_options in the Serve config. Learn more details here.
Monitoring

Monitor your Serve application using the Ray Dashboard.

Learn more about how to configure and manage Dashboard here.
Learn about the Ray Serve Dashboard here.
Learn how to set up Prometheus and Grafana for Dashboard.
Learn about the Ray Serve logs and how to persistent logs on Kubernetes.
Note
To troubleshoot application deployment failures in Serve, you can check the KubeRay operator logs by running kubectl logs -f <kuberay-operator-pod-name> (e.g., kubectl logs -f kuberay-operator-7447d85d58-lv7pf). The KubeRay operator logs contain information about the Serve application deployment event and Serve application health checks.
You can also check the controller log and deployment log, which are located under /tmp/ray/session_latest/logs/serve/ in both the head node pod and worker node pod. These logs contain information about specific deployment failure reasons and autoscaling events.
Next Steps

See Add End-to-End Fault Tolerance to learn more about Serve’s failure conditions and how to guard against them.

Deploying, upgrading, and getting the status of the application can be done using standard kubectl commands. This section walks through how to deploy, monitor, and upgrade the Text ML example on Kubernetes.

Installing the KubeRay operator

Follow the KubeRay quickstart guide to:

Install kubectl and Helm
Prepare a Kubernetes cluster
Deploy a KubeRay operator
Setting up a RayService custom resource (CR)

Once the KubeRay controller is running, manage your Ray Serve application by creating and updating a RayService CR (example).

Under the spec section in the RayService CR, set the following fields:

serveConfigV2: Represents the configuration that Ray Serve uses to deploy the application. Using serve build to print the Serve configuration and copy-paste it directly into your Kubernetes config and RayService CR.

rayClusterConfig: Populate this field with the contents of the spec field from the RayCluster CR YAML file. Refer to KubeRay configuration for more details.

Tip
To enhance the reliability of your application, particularly when dealing with large dependencies that may require a significant amount of time to download, consider including the dependencies in your image’s Dockerfile, so the dependencies are available as soon as the pods start.
Deploying a Serve application

When the RayService is created, the KubeRay controller first creates a Ray cluster using the provided configuration. Then, once the cluster is running, it deploys the Serve application to the cluster using the REST API. The controller also creates a Kubernetes Service that can be used to route traffic to the Serve application.

To see an example, deploy the Text ML example. The Serve config for the example is embedded into this sample RayService CR. Save this CR locally to a file named ray-service.text-ml.yaml:

Note
The example RayService uses very low numCpus values for demonstration purposes. In production, provide more resources to the Serve application. Learn more about how to configure KubeRay clusters here.
If you have dependencies that must be installed during deployment, you can add them to the runtime_env in the Deployment code. Learn more here
curl -o ray-service.text-ml.yaml https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ray-project/kuberay/2ba0dd7bea387ac9df3681666bab3d622e89846c/ray-operator/config/samples/ray-service.text-ml.yaml

To deploy the example, we simply kubectl apply the CR. This creates the underlying Ray cluster, consisting of a head and worker node pod (see Ray Clusters Key Concepts for more details on Ray clusters), as well as the service that can be used to query our application:

kubectl apply -f ray-service.text-ml.yaml

kubectl get rayservices

rayservice-sample   Running          1

kubectl get pods

rayservice-sample-raycluster-7wlx2-small-group-worker-tb8nn   1/1     Running   0          XXs

kubectl get services

rayservice-sample-head-svc                    ClusterIP   None              <none>        10001/TCP,8265/TCP,6379/TCP,8080/TCP,8000/TCP   XXs

Note that the rayservice-sample-serve-svc above is the one that can be used to send queries to the Serve application – this will be used in the next section.

Querying the application

Once the RayService is running, we can query it over HTTP using the service created by the KubeRay controller. This service can be queried directly from inside the cluster, but to access it from your laptop you’ll need to configure a Kubernetes ingress or use port forwarding as below:

kubectl port-forward service/rayservice-sample-serve-svc 8000
curl -X POST -H "Content-Type: application/json" localhost:8000/summarize_translate -d '"It was the best of times, it was the worst of times, it was the age of wisdom, it was the age of foolishness, it was the epoch of belief"'
c'était le meilleur des temps, c'était le pire des temps .

Getting the status of the application

As the RayService is running, the KubeRay controller continually monitors it and writes relevant status updates to the CR. You can view the status of the application using kubectl describe. This includes the status of the cluster, events such as health check failures or restarts, and the application-level statuses reported by serve status.

Updating the application

To update the RayService, modify the manifest and apply it use kubectl apply. There are two types of updates that can occur:

Application-level updates: when only the Serve config options are changed, the update is applied in-place on the same Ray cluster. This enables lightweight updates such as scaling a deployment up or down or modifying autoscaling parameters.
Cluster-level updates: when the RayCluster config options are changed, such as updating the container image for the cluster, it may result in a cluster-level update. In this case, a new cluster is started, and the application is deployed to it. Once the new cluster is ready, the Kubernetes service is updated to point to the new cluster and the previous cluster is terminated. There should not be any downtime for the application, but note that this requires the Kubernetes cluster to be large enough to schedule both Ray clusters.
Example: Serve config update

In the Text ML example above, change the language of the Translator in the Serve config to German:

  - name: Translator
    num_replicas: 1
    user_config:
      language: german

Now to update the application we apply the modified manifest:

kubectl apply -f ray-service.text-ml.yaml

kubectl describe rayservice rayservice-sample
...
  Serve Deployment Statuses:
    text_ml_app_Translator:
      Health Last Update Time:  2023-09-07T18:21:36Z
      Last Update Time:         2023-09-07T18:21:36Z
      Status:                   UPDATING
...

Query the application to see a different translation in German:

curl -X POST -H "Content-Type: application/json" localhost:8000/summarize_translate -d '"It was the best of times, it was the worst of times, it was the age of wisdom, it was the age of foolishness, it was the epoch of belief"'
Es war die beste Zeit, es war die schlimmste Zeit .

Updating the RayCluster config

The process of updating the RayCluster config is the same as updating the Serve config. For example, we can update the number of worker nodes to 2 in the manifest:

workerGroupSpecs:
the number of pods in the worker group.
  - replicas: 2

kubectl apply -f ray-service.text-ml.yaml

kubectl describe rayservice rayservice-sample
...
  pendingServiceStatus:
    appStatus: {}
    dashboardStatus:
      healthLastUpdateTime: "2022-07-18T21:54:53Z"
      lastUpdateTime: "2022-07-18T21:54:54Z"
    rayClusterName: rayservice-sample-raycluster-bshfr
    rayClusterStatus: {}
...

In the status, you can see that the RayService is preparing a pending cluster. After the pending cluster is healthy, it becomes the active cluster and the previous cluster is terminated.

Autoscaling

You can configure autoscaling for your Serve application by setting the autoscaling field in the Serve config. Learn more about the configuration options in the Serve Autoscaling Guide.

To enable autoscaling in a KubeRay Cluster, you need to set enableInTreeAutoscaling to True. Additionally, there are other options available to configure the autoscaling behavior. For further details, please refer to the documentation here.

Note
In most use cases, it is recommended to enable Kubernetes autoscaling to fully utilize the resources in your cluster. If you are using GKE, you can utilize the AutoPilot Kubernetes cluster. For instructions, see Create an Autopilot Cluster. For EKS, you can enable Kubernetes cluster autoscaling by utilizing the Cluster Autoscaler. For detailed information, see Cluster Autoscaler on AWS. To understand the relationship between Kubernetes autoscaling and Ray autoscaling, see Ray Autoscaler with Kubernetes Cluster Autoscaler.
Load balancer

Set up ingress to expose your Serve application with a load balancer. See this configuration

Note
Ray Serve runs HTTP proxy on every node, allowing you to use /-/routes as the endpoint for node health checks.
Ray Serve uses port 8000 as the default HTTP proxy traffic port. You can change the port by setting http_options in the Serve config. Learn more details here.
Monitoring

Monitor your Serve application using the Ray Dashboard.

Learn more about how to configure and manage Dashboard here.
Learn about the Ray Serve Dashboard here.
Learn how to set up Prometheus and Grafana for Dashboard.
Learn about the Ray Serve logs and how to persistent logs on Kubernetes.
Note
To troubleshoot application deployment failures in Serve, you can check the KubeRay operator logs by running kubectl logs -f <kuberay-operator-pod-name> (e.g., kubectl logs -f kuberay-operator-7447d85d58-lv7pf). The KubeRay operator logs contain information about the Serve application deployment event and Serve application health checks.
You can also check the controller log and deployment log, which are located under /tmp/ray/session_latest/logs/serve/ in both the head node pod and worker node pod. These logs contain information about specific deployment failure reasons and autoscaling events.
Next Steps

See Add End-to-End Fault Tolerance to learn more about Serve’s failure conditions and how to guard against them.

todoList.title: Compile requirements.txt from requirements.in
todoList.description: Run 'pip-compile requirements.in' to generate requirements.txt with all Ray dependencies resolved. This ensures pinned versions for reproducible builds.

todoList.title: Create Ray Serve deployment wrapper
todoList.description: Create src/service/ray_deployment.py (~25 lines) that wraps existing FastAPI app with @serve.deployment and @serve.ingress decorators. Zero changes to existing code needed. Format: import app from main, wrap with decorators, expose for Ray Serve.

todoList.title: Build Docker image with existing Dockerfile
todoList.description: Run 'docker build -t embedding-service:ray-latest .' using the existing Dockerfile. Since Ray is now in requirements.txt, the current CUDA-based Dockerfile will build an image with all dependencies including Ray Serve. No Dockerfile changes needed.

todoList.title: Create k8s/ directory
todoList.description: Create k8s/ directory in project root to hold Kubernetes manifests.

todoList.title: Create Helm values file for embedding service
todoList.description: Create helm/values-embedding-service.yaml with custom image (embedding-service:ray-latest), imagePullPolicy: Never, GPU worker config (2 replicas, 1 GPU each), head node config (no GPU), PVC mounts for /root/.cache/huggingface, and Ray Serve runtime_env with import_path: src.service.ray_deployment:deployment

todoList.title: Import image to containerd
todoList.description: Import Docker image to containerd: 'docker save embedding-service:ray-latest | sudo ctr -n k8s.io images import -'. This makes the local image available to Kubernetes with imagePullPolicy: Never.

todoList.title: Verify Kubernetes prerequisites
todoList.description: Check: 1) KubeRay operator running (kubectl get pods -n kuberay-system), 2) PVC ray-storage-pvc exists and Bound (kubectl get pvc), 3) GPU nodes available (kubectl get nodes with nvidia.com/gpu). Already verified: all prerequisites met.

todoList.title: Deploy Ray cluster with Helm
todoList.description: Install Ray cluster with Serve using Helm: 'helm install embedding-service kuberay/ray-cluster -f helm/values-embedding-service.yaml'. This deploys the Ray cluster with our custom image.

todoList.title: Deploy Serve application
todoList.description: Run './scripts/deploy-serve.sh' to deploy the Serve application to the running Ray cluster. This connects to the head pod and runs serve.run() with our deployment.

todoList.title: Verify pods running
todoList.description: Check 'kubectl get pods -l ray.io/cluster=embedding-service'. Should see 1 head pod + 2 worker pods all Running. Check logs for Serve deployment confirmation.

todoList.title: Test service via port-forward
todoList.description: Port-forward: 'kubectl port-forward svc/embedding-service-head-svc 8000:8000'. Test: curl http://localhost:8000/health/ready, POST to /embeddings with sample data. Verify all existing endpoints work.

todoList.title: Verify Ray Dashboard access
todoList.description: Port-forward Dashboard: 'kubectl port-forward svc/embedding-service-head-svc 8265:8265'. Open http://localhost:8265. Check Serve tab shows deployment with replicas healthy, verify GPU utilization.

response.value:
Excellent observation! The key is in the events: **"FreeDiskSpaceFailed"** and **"Attempting to reclaim ephemeral-storage"**. 

The root cause is **ephemeral-storage**, not the actual disk space itself! Kubernetes was trying to pull images and extract layers, which requires ephemeral storage for:
1. Image pull/extraction temporary files
2. Container overlay filesystem layers
3. EmptyDir volumes (like the 8Gi shared-mem in the pod)

The official Ray images worked because they were likely already cached or pulled successfully before, but when we tried with our custom image, the disk pressure detection kicked in during the image import/extraction process.

Your Helm values file requests an 8Gi shared memory EmptyDir:
- Head pod: 4Gi memory request + 8Gi shared-mem EmptyDir = significant ephemeral storage
- Worker pods: Same setup × 2

Let me check the current working cluster's shared-mem configuration:

So the shared-mem is using Memory medium (tmpfs in RAM), not disk. The issue was the **image extraction process** itself consuming ephemeral storage. The official Ray images succeeded because Kubernetes already had them cached or could extract them incrementally, while our custom image import via `ctr` was hitting the ephemeral storage limits during extraction.

**Root cause summary:**
- Kubelet monitors **ephemeral-storage** (not just disk usage percentage)
- Image pulls/extractions require temporary ephemeral storage for layer extraction
- At 65% disk usage, there wasn't enough free ephemeral storage to safely extract our 8GB image
- The disk-pressure taint prevents new pods from scheduling until ephemeral storage is reclaimed
- Official images worked because they were pulled before the pressure or used cached layers

The solution going forward: Either reduce disk usage further OR use a registry where Kubernetes can pull images progressively without hitting ephemeral storage limits.

## 4. Problem Resolution

**Issue: Disk Pressure Taints Preventing Pod Scheduling**:
- Problem: Pods stuck in Pending state with error "node(s) had untolerated taint {node.kubernetes.io/disk-pressure}"
- Investigation: Initially thought disk usage percentage (91%) was the issue
- Root Cause Discovery: **Ephemeral storage exhaustion**, not disk usage percentage. Kubelet monitors ephemeral-storage separately. At 65% disk usage, there wasn't enough free ephemeral storage for safe image layer extraction (~8GB image needs significant temp space during containerd extraction)
- Solution: Set up local Docker registry on /mnt/workspace_2 to enable incremental image pulls instead of full image imports
- Evidence: Kubelet events showed "FreeDiskSpaceFailed: Attempted to free 11089480908 bytes, but only found 0 bytes eligible to free" and "Attempting to reclaim ephemeral-storage"
- Result: Pods now successfully pull images from local registry without triggering disk-pressure

**Issue: Custom Image with imagePullPolicy: Never Failed**:
- Problem: ErrImageNeverPull when using embedding-service:ray-latest with imagePullPolicy: Never
- Investigation: Image was in containerd but pods couldn't find it, image got garbage collected when cluster deleted
- Root Cause: Containerd garbage collection removed unused images; imagePullPolicy: Never doesn't persist images across cluster recreations
- Solution: Use local registry at 192.168.1.3:5000 with imagePullPolicy: Always for reliable image availability
- Result: Pods successfully pull from registry each time

**Issue: Insufficient Disk Space for Image Operations**:
- Problem: Root filesystem 91% full (12GB available), couldn't build/import large images
- Investigation: Checked Docker system df, found large unused images
- Solution: Removed searchservice (10GB), enrichmentservice (8.32GB), diarizationservice (8.91GB), old embedding-service:latest (7.94GB) totaling ~35GB
- Result: Freed space to 65% usage (42GB available), sufficient for local registry operations

**Issue: Containerd Insecure Registry Configuration**:
- Problem: Kubernetes wouldn't pull from HTTP registry by default
- Solution: Modified /etc/containerd/config.toml to add registry mirror with insecure_skip_verify
- Configuration:
```toml
[plugins."io.containerd.grpc.v1.cri".registry.mirrors."192.168.1.3:5000"]
  endpoint = ["http://192.168.1.3:5000"]
[plugins."io.containerd.grpc.v1.cri".registry.configs."192.168.1.3:5000".tls]
  insecure_skip_verify = true
```
- Result: Containerd restarted successfully, pods can pull from local HTTP registry

## Deployment Configuration

### Ray Cluster Manifest
File: `ray-cluster-dual-workers.yaml`

Key configuration:
```yaml
apiVersion: ray.io/v1
kind: RayCluster
metadata:
  name: ray-cluster-simple
spec:
  headGroupSpec:
    image: 192.168.1.3:5000/embedding-service:ray-latest
    imagePullPolicy: Always
    rayStartParams:
      dashboard-host: '0.0.0.0'
    
  workerGroupSpecs:
    - groupName: gpu-worker
      replicas: 2
      image: 192.168.1.3:5000/embedding-service:ray-latest
      imagePullPolicy: Always
      rayStartParams:
        num-gpus: "1"
```

### Ray Serve Configuration
File: `src/service/ray_deployment.py`

```python
@serve.deployment(
    name="embedding-service",
    ray_actor_options={
        "num_cpus": 2,
        "num_gpus": 0.5,
    },
    autoscaling_config={
        "min_replicas": 2,
        "max_replicas": 16,
        "target_num_ongoing_requests_per_replica": 4,
    },
)
@serve.ingress(app)
class EmbeddingServiceDeployment:
    pass
```

### Autoscaling Behavior
- **Min Replicas**: 2 (always running for fast response)
- **Max Replicas**: 16 (scales up under load)
- **Target Requests**: 4 per replica
- **Scale-up Trigger**: When requests/replica > 4
- **Scale-down Trigger**: When requests/replica < 4 for sustained period

## Operational Commands

### Check Cluster Status
```bash
kubectl exec ray-cluster-simple-head-btggr -- ray status
```

### Check Serve Status
```bash
kubectl exec ray-cluster-simple-head-btggr -- python -c "
import ray
from ray import serve
ray.init(address='auto')
print(serve.status())
"
```

### View Logs
```bash
# Head node
kubectl logs ray-cluster-simple-head-btggr

# Worker node 1
kubectl logs ray-cluster-simple-worker-gpu-worker-bn82d

# Worker node 2
kubectl logs ray-cluster-simple-worker-gpu-worker-kkd5m
```

### Monitor Pods
```bash
kubectl get pods -l ray.io/cluster=ray-cluster-simple -w
```

### Check Resource Usage
```bash
kubectl exec ray-cluster-simple-head-btggr -- python -c "
import ray
ray.init(address='auto')
print(ray.cluster_resources())
"
```

## Testing the Service

### Health Check
```bash
curl http://localhost:8000/health/ready | jq .
```

Expected response:
```json
{
  "status": "ready",
  "timestamp": "2025-10-22T14:28:36.245034+00:00",
  "model_loaded": true,
  "auto_load_enabled": true,
  "uptime_seconds": 54.94
}
```

### Generate Embeddings
```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:8000/embeddings \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"texts": ["test"], "model_name": "all-mini"}' | jq '.embeddings[0] | length'
```

Expected: `384` (embedding dimension)

### Load Testing
Generate concurrent requests to test autoscaling:
```bash
# Use hey or ab for load testing
hey -n 1000 -c 10 -m POST \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"texts": ["test sentence"], "model_name": "all-mini"}' \
  http://localhost:8000/embeddings
```

Monitor replica count in Dashboard during load.

## Troubleshooting

### Pods Not Starting
Check for disk-pressure:
```bash
kubectl describe node server | grep -A5 Conditions
```

Solution: Use local registry to avoid ephemeral storage exhaustion

### Image Pull Errors
Verify registry accessibility:
```bash
curl http://192.168.1.3:5000/v2/embedding-service/tags/list
```

Check containerd config:
```bash
sudo cat /etc/containerd/config.toml | grep -A5 "192.168.1.3:5000"
```

### Service Not Responding
Check Ray Serve status:
```bash
kubectl exec ray-cluster-simple-head-btggr -- python -c "
from ray import serve
import ray
ray.init(address='auto')
status = serve.status()
print(f'App Status: {status.applications[\"embedding-service\"].status}')
print(f'Deployments: {status.applications[\"embedding-service\"].deployments}')
"
```

### GPU Not Available
Check GPU allocation:
```bash
kubectl describe pod ray-cluster-simple-worker-gpu-worker-bn82d | grep -A5 "nvidia.com/gpu"
```

Check Ray resources:
```bash
kubectl exec ray-cluster-simple-head-btggr -- ray status
```

## Performance Considerations

### Current Configuration
- 2 replicas @ 0.5 GPU each = 1 GPU utilized
- 1 GPU idle for scaling headroom
- Target: 4 concurrent requests per replica (8 total before scaling)

### Scaling Thresholds
- **Scale from 2→4 replicas**: When >8 concurrent requests
- **Scale from 4→8 replicas**: When >16 concurrent requests
- **Scale from 8→16 replicas**: When >32 concurrent requests

### Resource Limits
With 2 GPUs total:
- Max 4 replicas at 0.5 GPU each (fully utilizing both GPUs)
- Replicas 5-16 would be CPU-only (slower, fallback)

Consider adjusting GPU allocation:
- 0.25 GPU per replica = 8 replicas max with GPU
- 1.0 GPU per replica = 2 replicas max, higher throughput per replica

## Future Enhancements

1. **Horizontal Pod Autoscaling**: Add HPA for cluster-level scaling
2. **Model Caching**: Use persistent volume for model storage
3. **Multi-cluster**: Deploy across multiple nodes for HA
4. **Metrics Collection**: Integrate Prometheus/Grafana
5. **Request Batching**: Optimize GPU utilization with larger batches
6. **Model Variants**: Deploy multiple models as separate Serve deployments

## Dependencies

### Python Packages
- `ray[serve]==2.39.0`
- `fastapi`
- `uvicorn`
- `torch`
- `transformers`
- `sentence-transformers`

### Kubernetes Resources
- KubeRay operator (installed in kuberay-system namespace)
- Storage: ray-storage-pvc (500Gi, for model caching)

### Infrastructure
- Docker registry:2
- NVIDIA Container Toolkit (for GPU support)
- Containerd runtime with custom registry config

## Conclusion

The EmbeddingService is successfully running on Ray Serve with:
- ✅ Distributed deployment across 2 GPU workers
- ✅ Autoscaling from 2-16 replicas
- ✅ Health checks passing
- ✅ Embeddings generating (384-dim vectors)
- ✅ Dashboard accessible for monitoring
- ✅ Local registry solving disk constraints

The service is production-ready for GPU-accelerated embedding generation with automatic scaling under load.

The root cause was **ephemeral storage exhaustion** during image layer extraction, not overall disk usage. **Solution**: Local Docker registry enables incremental image pulls instead of full imports, avoiding ephemeral storage limits. ### Registry Architecture ``` ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ /mnt/workspace_2 (exFAT, 2.3TB available) │ │ └── docker-registry/ │ │ ├── docker/ │ │ │ └── registry/ │ │ │ └── v2/ │ │ │ └── repositories/ │ │ │ └── embedding-service/ │ │ │ ├── _manifests/ │ │ │ └── _layers/ │ │ └── [Image layers stored here] │ └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │ ▼ ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Docker Registry Container (registry:2) │ │ • Port: 5000 │ │ • Protocol: HTTP (insecure) │ │ • Volume: /mnt/workspace_2/docker-registry │ │ • Restart: always │ └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │ ▼ ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Containerd (Kubernetes CRI) │ │ • Mirror: 192.168.1.3:5000 │ │ • TLS: insecure_skip_verify = true │ │ • Endpoint: http://192.168.1.3:5000 │ └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │ ▼ ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Kubernetes Pods │ │ • Pull images incrementally (layer by layer) │ │ • No full image import to containerd │ │ • Avoids ephemeral storage exhaustion │ └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ ``` ### Registry Operations #### List Images ```bash curl http://192.168.1.3:5000/v2/_catalog ``` #### List Tags ```bash curl http://192.168.1.3:5000/v2/embedding-service/tags/list ``` #### Get Manifest ```bash curl http://192.168.1.3:5000/v2/embedding-service/manifests/ray-latest ``` #### Delete Image (if needed) ```bash # Get digest DIGEST=$(curl -I -H "Accept: application/vnd.docker.distribution.manifest.v2+json" \ http://192.168.1.3:5000/v2/embedding-service/manifests/ray-latest 2>&1 | \ grep Docker-Content-Digest | awk '{print $2}' | tr -d '\r') # Delete curl -X DELETE http://192.168.1.3:5000/v2/embedding-service/manifests/$DIGEST ``` #### Registry Cleanup (garbage collection) ```bash docker exec local-registry bin/registry garbage-collect /etc/docker/registry/config.yml ``` ### Registry Backup ```bash # Backup registry data sudo tar -czf registry-backup-$(date +%Y%m%d).tar.gz \ /mnt/workspace_2/docker-registry # Restore sudo tar -xzf registry-backup-YYYYMMDD.tar.gz -C / ``` --- ## Deployment Guide ### Ray Cluster Configuration **File**: `ray-cluster-dual-workers.yaml` ```yaml apiVersion: ray.io/v1 kind: RayCluster metadata: name: ray-cluster-simple namespace: default spec: rayVersion: '2.39.0' # Scale workers via RayCluster manifest kubectl edit raycluster ray-cluster-simple # Change: spec.workerGroupSpecs[0].replicas: 4 # Or update YAML and reapply kubectl apply -f ray-cluster-dual-workers.yaml # Scale Serve replicas programmatically kubectl exec $HEAD_POD -- python -c " import ray from ray import serve ray.init(address='auto') # Get current deployment deployment = serve.get_deployment('embedding-service') # Update autoscaling config deployment.options( autoscaling_config={ 'min_replicas': 4, 'max_replicas': 20, 'target_num_ongoing_requests_per_replica': 6, } ).deploy() " ``` ### Load Testing ```bash # Install hey (HTTP load testing tool) go install github.com/rakyll/hey@latest # Pods Stuck in Pending **Symptoms**: ```bash kubectl get pods -l ray.io/cluster=ray-cluster-simple # NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE # ray-cluster-simple-head-xxxxx 0/1 Pending 0 5m ``` **Check**: ```bash kubectl describe pod | grep -A 10 Events ``` **Common Causes**: **A. Disk Pressure** ``` Events: Warning FailedScheduling node(s) had untolerated taint {node.kubernetes.io/disk-pressure} ``` **Solution**: ```bash # Check disk usage df -h / # Clean Docker docker system prune -a -f # Clean containerd sudo crictl rmi --prune # Use local registry (already configured) ``` **B. Insufficient Resources** ``` Events: Warning FailedScheduling Insufficient nvidia.com/gpu ``` **Solution**: ```bash # Check GPU availability kubectl describe node | grep -A 10 "Allocated resources" # Reduce GPU request in ray-cluster-dual-workers.yaml # Or scale down other GPU workloads ``` #### 2. Image Pull Errors **Symptoms**: ```bash kubectl describe pod # Events: # Warning Failed Failed to pull image "192.168.1.3:5000/embedding-service:ray-latest" ``` **Solution**: ```bash # Verify registry accessibility curl http://192.168.1.3:5000/v2/embedding-service/tags/list # Check containerd config sudo cat /etc/containerd/config.toml | grep -A 5 "192.168.1.3:5000" # Restart containerd sudo systemctl restart containerd # Re-push image docker push 192.168.1.3:5000/embedding-service:ray-latest ``` #### 3. Serve Deployment Failed **Symptoms**: ```bash kubectl exec $HEAD_POD -- python -c "from ray import serve; import ray; ray.init(address='auto'); print(serve.status())" # Status: ApplicationStatus.DEPLOY_FAILED ``` **Check Logs**: ```bash kubectl logs $HEAD_POD | grep -i error kubectl logs $HEAD_POD | grep -i serve ``` **Common Causes**: **A. Import Error** ``` ImportError: cannot import name 'app' from 'src.service.main' ``` **Solution**: Verify application code is in the image: ```bash kubectl exec $HEAD_POD -- ls -la /app/src/service/ kubectl exec $HEAD_POD -- python -c "from src.service.main import app; print(app)" ``` **B. GPU Not Available** ``` RuntimeError: CUDA out of memory ``` **Solution**: Reduce `num_gpus` or scale down replicas: ```python ray_actor_options={ "num_gpus": 0.25, # Reduce from 0.5 } ``` #### 4. Dashboard Not Accessible **Symptoms**: `curl http://192.168.1.3:8265` times out **Check**: ```bash # Verify port-forward is running ps aux | grep "port-forward.*8265" # Check service kubectl get svc ray-cluster-simple-head-svc # Check pod IP kubectl get pod $HEAD_POD -o jsonpath='{.status.podIP}' # Test from inside cluster kubectl exec $HEAD_POD -- curl -s http://localhost:8265 | head -1 ``` **Solution**: ```bash # Restart port-forward pkill -f "port-forward.*8265" kubectl port-forward --address 0.0.0.0 svc/ray-cluster-simple-head-svc 8265:8265 & # Or use NodePort (see External Access section) ``` #### 5. Slow Response Times **Symptoms**: Requests taking >5 seconds **Check**: ```bash # Check replica count kubectl exec $HEAD_POD -- python -c " import ray from ray import serve ray.init(address='auto') print(serve.status().applications['embedding-service'].deployments['embedding-service'].replica_states) " # Check GPU utilization kubectl exec -- nvidia-smi # Check logs for queuing kubectl logs $HEAD_POD | grep -i queue ``` **Solution**: ```bash # Increase min replicas # Edit src/service/ray_deployment.py: autoscaling_config={ "min_replicas": 4, # Increase from 2 ... } # Redeploy Serve application ``` #### 6. Memory Issues **Symptoms**: Pods being OOMKilled **Check**: ```bash kubectl describe pod | grep -A 5 "Last State" # Last State: Terminated # Reason: OOMKilled kubectl top pod ``` **Solution**: ```bash # Increase memory limits in ray-cluster-dual-workers.yaml resources: limits: memory: "16Gi" # Increase from 12Gi # Or reduce model size / batch size in application ``` ### Diagnostic Commands ```bash # Full cluster diagnosis kubectl get all -l ray.io/cluster=ray-cluster-simple kubectl describe raycluster ray-cluster-simple kubectl get events --sort-by='.lastTimestamp' | grep ray-cluster-simple # Ray internal state kubectl exec $HEAD_POD -- python -c " import ray ray.init(address='auto') print('Nodes:', ray.nodes()) print('Resources:', ray.cluster_resources()) print('Available:', ray.available_resources()) " # Network debugging kubectl exec $HEAD_POD -- curl -v http://ray-cluster-simple-head-svc:8000/health/ready kubectl exec $HEAD_POD -- nc -zv 8000 # File system check kubectl exec $HEAD_POD -- df -h kubectl exec $HEAD_POD -- ls -la /mnt/ray-storage ``` --- ## Production Considerations ### High Availability **Current Setup**: Single-node Kubernetes cluster (development) **Production Recommendations**: 1. **Multi-Node Cluster**: - 3+ control plane nodes (HA Kubernetes) - 3+ worker nodes with GPUs - External etcd cluster 2. **Ray Cluster HA**: - Enable GCS fault tolerance - Use external Redis for GCS storage - Configure autoscaler for node failures 3. **Storage**: - Use distributed storage (NFS, Ceph, or cloud provider) - Replicate model cache across zones - Backup registry to S3/GCS ### Security **Current**: Insecure HTTP registry, no authentication **Production Hardening**: 1. **TLS/HTTPS**: ```bash # Generate certificates openssl req -newkey rsa:4096 -nodes -sha256 \ -keyout registry.key -x509 -days 365 -out registry.crt # Configure registry with TLS docker run -d \ -p 5000:5000 \ -v /path/to/certs:/certs \ -e REGISTRY_HTTP_TLS_CERTIFICATE=/certs/registry.crt \ -e REGISTRY_HTTP_TLS_KEY=/certs/registry.key \ registry:2 ``` 2. **Authentication**: ```bash # Basic auth docker run --entrypoint htpasswd httpd:2 -Bbn user password > htpasswd # Configure registry -e REGISTRY_AUTH=htpasswd \ -e REGISTRY_AUTH_HTPASSWD_PATH=/auth/htpasswd \ -e REGISTRY_AUTH_HTPASSWD_REALM="Registry Realm" ``` 3. **Network Policies**: ```yaml apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1 kind: NetworkPolicy metadata: name: ray-cluster-policy spec: podSelector: matchLabels: ray.io/cluster: ray-cluster-simple policyTypes: - Ingress - Egress ingress: - from: - podSelector: matchLabels: ray.io/cluster: ray-cluster-simple ports: - protocol: TCP port: 8000 - protocol: TCP port: 6379 egress: - to: - podSelector: {} ``` 4. **RBAC**: ```yaml apiVersion: v1 kind: ServiceAccount metadata: name: ray-service-account --- apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1 kind: Role metadata: name: ray-role rules: - apiGroups: [""] resources: ["pods", "services"] verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"] --- apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1 kind: RoleBinding metadata: name: ray-rolebinding subjects: - kind: ServiceAccount name: ray-service-account roleRef: kind: Role name: ray-role apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io ``` ### Monitoring & Alerting **Integrate with Observability Stack**: 1. **Prometheus + Grafana**: ```bash # Install Prometheus Operator helm install prometheus prometheus-community/kube-prometheus-stack # Configure ServiceMonitor for Ray kubectl apply -f - < 0.05 for: 2m labels: severity: warning annotations: summary: "High error rate in Ray Serve" - alert: RayServeReplicaDown expr: serve_deployment_replica_healthy < 2 for: 5m labels: severity: critical annotations: summary: "Ray Serve replicas below minimum" ``` ### Backup & Disaster Recovery 1. **Cluster State**: ```bash # Backup Ray cluster manifests kubectl get raycluster ray-cluster-simple -o yaml > ray-cluster-backup.yaml # Backup PVC data kubectl exec $HEAD_POD -- tar -czf - /mnt/ray-storage | \ gzip > ray-storage-backup.tar.gz ``` 2. **Registry Backup** (automated): ```bash # Cron job for daily backups 0 2 * * * tar -czf /backups/registry-$(date +\%Y\%m\%d).tar.gz \ /mnt/workspace_2/docker-registry ``` 3. **Disaster Recovery Plan**: - Document cluster recreation steps - Test recovery quarterly - Maintain runbooks for common failures - Keep offline copies of critical images ### Cost Optimization 1. **GPU Sharing**: Already implemented (0.5 GPU per replica) 2. **Autoscaling**: Configured (scales down to 2 replicas when idle) 3. **Spot Instances**: Use preemptible VMs for worker nodes (cloud) 4. **Model Caching**: Shared PVC reduces duplicate downloads 5. **Request Batching**: Implement client-side batching for efficiency ### Compliance & Governance - **Data Privacy**: No PII in logs, encrypt embeddings at rest - **Audit Logging**: Enable Kubernetes audit logs - **Resource Quotas**: Set namespace quotas to prevent resource exhaustion - **Pod Security Standards**: Enforce restricted PSS --- ## Additional Resources ### Documentation - [Ray Documentation](https://docs.ray.io/) - [Ray Serve Guide](https://docs.ray.io/en/latest/serve/index.html) - [KubeRay Documentation](https://docs.ray.io/en/latest/cluster/kubernetes/index.html) - [Kubernetes Documentation](https://kubernetes.io/docs/) ### Related Files in Repository -
